newsitem.title: USA: U.S experts eye rand risks amid S. African reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S experts eye rand risks amid S. African reforms.

text.p: Even as South Africa's valiant struggle to build a prosperous democracy inspires growing confidence, U.S. experts warned political and speculative risks still pose a material threat to the value of the rand.

"Obviously, you can see progress written all over South Africa," said Karanta Kalley, director of the Middle East and Africa Service of the WEFA Group. "But at the same time you've got to understand that the fact that progress is taking place does not mean that some of the core problems, risk related issues are totally out of the way."
Kalley said improvement in macroeconomic fundamentals has not immunized the rand from speculative attacks or occasional bouts of political instability.

While Kalley noted the recognition in some circles of Thabo Mbeki, executive deputy president of South Africa, as President Nelson Mandela's heir apparent, he said political risk remains "very high." He pointed to the large population of black South Africans that still live in poverty despite some gains through empowerment measures.
Last year, concern over dwindling foreign exchange reserves, which can invite speculative attacks, battered the rand. It depreciated nearly 30 percent against the dollar.
Yet the rand has improved recently from its 1996 year-end rate of 4.68, trading near 4.6050/00 per dollar on Friday, up from 4.6255/6305 late Thursday. Gains followed a flood of good news this week.
South Africa's cabinet deferred a decision on an arms sale to Syria that threatened to cause a cutoff in U.S. aid to South Africa.
Next, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals told Reuters that the rand could prove "very stable" in 1997, aided by a sharply better balance of payments position.
Close on the heels of the Stals interview came news that South Africa's trade surplus unexpectedly ballooned to more than two billion rand ($432.8 million) in December.
Indications that some investors have adopted a more upbeat outlook on the currency have emerged in the bond market.
"A sign of greater confidence in the rand is the demand for longer duration paper that we're seeing," said a trader at a major investment bank in New York.
"So, if that's an indication of money that's there to stay, we've been seeing quite a bit of interest in longer-dated rand," the trader said.
Still, the trader expressed concern about South Africa's "miniscule" foreign currency reserves saying "that could be a wild card."
The South African government is currently attempting to implement a series of fiscal and economic reforms aimed at steering the economy down the right track.

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel has said South Africa is committed to real state spending cuts to reduce the budget deficit to 4.0 percent of gross domestic product in the 1997/98 financial year and 3.0 percent over the following two years.
But Manuel ruled out tax increases, saying the spending cuts would have to be accompanied by improved tax collection in order to achieve targeted deficits.

Guido Cipriani, director of the sovereign ratings group at Standard and Poor's Corp, expressed doubt in a government's ability to gain significant ground through tax collection measures which have proven to be a "very slow and disappointing" effort around the world.
He said S&P is sympathetic with the view the rand had declined by more than what appears to be consistent with exchange rate fundamentals.

"However, over a short period of time, there still can be further downward pressure on the exchange rate...until people gain full confidence that the government is managing the process well (and) that the economy is going to respond to the measures that have been adopted," Cipriani said.
S&P does not make currency forecasts, but it evaluates all aspects of an economy to determine debt service capacity.
S&P rates South Africa's long-term local currency debt at BBB-plus and long-term foreign currency debt at BB-plus. Both have a positive ratings outlook.
Meanwhile, Kalley said the WEFA Group forecast sees the rand around 4.86 to 4.90 per dollar by the end of the year, with an average forecast of 4.76.
